transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well, I decided to finally make an appointment because... it's just been really frustrating lately. I keep getting these, um, these nagging thoughts that I forgot something really, really important. 

I teach third grade—well, sometimes fourth depending on the district's needs, but right now it's third—and I'll be at home in the evening, just trying to unwind, and suddenly this thought just hits me that I didn't set up my classroom materials safely. Like, maybe I left the pointy scissors out near the edge of the activity table, or the heavy supply bins aren't pushed back all the way and one of the kids is going to trip and get hurt. 

And it's not just at school, it happens with my family too. I help out with my aunt, and I'll get this intense feeling out of nowhere that I left her medicine out wrong. Like, maybe I set the wrong bottle on the counter for her, or I left the cap loose, or I mixed up the morning and evening ones. And the really frustrating part is, logically, I know I probably handled it fine. I'm a very organized person, I really am, and I pay attention to what I'm doing. But the doubt just keeps popping back into my head, over and over. I'll just be sitting there trying to watch a show or eat dinner, and my brain is just stuck on that medicine bottle or those classroom supplies, and I just can't shake the feeling that I messed it up somehow. It just won't let it go.

When these thoughts come up, do you find yourself doing certain things over and over again, like checking the classroom supplies or medicine bottles, to try to ease the worry or make sure everything is safe?

Yes, exactly. That's exactly what happens, and it's like I just can't walk away until I'm absolutely sure, even though, like I said, I know I already did it right. So, before I leave the classroom at the end of the day—usually around 3:45, because the kids leave at 3:15 and I try to use that half hour to prep—I'll pack up my bag, put my coat on, and then I just have to go back and check. I'll walk around the activity tables to look at the supply bins, and then I'll check my lesson plans on my desk to make sure I didn't leave any confidential student notes out, and then I'll go back to the supply bins again. I just... I go back over the exact same things a few times. 

And it's the exact same way at home or at my aunt's. Before I leave her house, I'll stare at her pill organizer, making sure the little plastic lids for the day are snapped shut, and I'll check her stove to make sure the dials are all pointing straight up to 'off'. I'll check the stove, then the pills, then the stove again. 

And even when I finally leave, like when I'm in my car driving away, sometimes I have to silently replay exactly what I did in my head. I'll picture my hand turning the stove knob, or I'll picture the scissors safely put away in the drawer, just playing the memory over and over in my mind. I have to keep replaying it or checking the physical items until I finally get this specific feeling... like I just have to do it until I feel calm enough to actually move on with my day. And honestly, it's becoming a real problem because it makes me run late sometimes. Just last week, I was supposed to meet a friend for coffee at 4:30 and I didn't get there until almost 5:00 because I got stuck in the classroom doing my rounds, just checking and rechecking the same things because my brain wouldn't give me that calm feeling. It's just so exhausting to have to do that.
Have these thoughts and the things you do to try to calm them down started to interfere with your job, relationships, or other important parts of your life?

Well, it's... I mean, I'm still getting through everything I need to do. I haven't missed any days of work or anything drastic like that, and I'm still showing up for my aunt and my family. But it's just... it's definitely making things harder, you know? Like, my mornings just take so much longer now. I try to be out the door by 7:15 so I can get to school, get my coffee from the staff room, and be completely settled before the bell rings, but lately, because of all the checking I have to do before I leave my own house—making sure the coffee maker is off, checking the locks, making sure my straightener is unplugged, which I'll check like three times—I end up leaving late. And then I hit the school zone traffic, and by the time I actually walk into my classroom, I'm feeling so rushed and behind before the day has even officially started. It's like I'm already playing catch-up at 8:00 AM. 

And then my lesson prep, which I usually really enjoy—I love finding new activities for the kids, especially for science units—it just doesn't feel as smooth. I'm distracted. I'm sitting there trying to cut out laminations or organize folders, and half my brain is still stuck on whether I locked my front door properly or if I left a pen uncapped that's going to dry out and ruin the desk. Even in the evenings, I usually try to do some journaling to unwind. I've kept a journal since I was in high school, and it's always been my quiet time, my restorative time. But lately, I'll be trying to write, and I just can't focus on it because I'm replaying the mental images of my classroom or my aunt's stove. It's just... it's taking the joy out of the things that usually help me relax, and making the everyday stuff feel like a chore. So, I'm managing, I'm functioning, but it's just... it's a lot of extra weight to carry around all the time.

Have these thoughts and behaviors ever made it difficult for you to engage in social activities, caused problems at work beyond the stress you’ve described, or affected any of your relationships with friends or family?

Well, like I was kind of saying just a minute ago, I really am still getting through all my main work and family commitments. I haven't, you know, been written up by my principal or gotten into any huge fights with my friends or my aunt. I'm still doing exactly what I need to do on paper. 

But... well, I guess the problem at work isn't that I'm failing at my job, it's just that, like I mentioned, my mornings take so much longer now. And I know I just talked about this, but it really is the biggest hurdle for me right now—I arrive at school feeling so incredibly rushed and behind before the day even officially starts. Usually, before the bell rings, that's the time I'd be chatting with the other teachers in the hallway, you know, catching up on their weekends, building those work relationships. But lately, instead of doing that, I'm practically sprinting to my classroom because I lost twenty minutes checking the straightener and the locks at home. I just don't have the time to be social at work anymore because I'm always playing catch-up.

And then with my friends and my family... I mean, I still see them. I'm still showing up for coffee dates, even if I'm late sometimes, and I'm still taking care of my aunt. But I'm just not as *present*, I guess? Because, like I said with my lesson prep, or even just my evening journaling which has always been my absolute favorite way to decompress, it just doesn't feel as smooth or restorative as it used to. I'm sitting there trying to write, or I'm sitting there trying to have a conversation with a friend, and my brain is just somewhere else entirely. 

So I haven't lost any friends over it, and my job is safe, but it's just... it's draining. I used to really love those quiet moments in the evening, picking out my favorite colored pens for my journal, writing down the little funny things the third graders said that day, really reflecting on things. And now I just sit there and stare at the blank page and replay images of my aunt's stove knobs or my classroom scissors. So, no, no major disasters or broken relationships, but it's just this constant, exhausting drag on my day.
Do these thoughts and the things you do to manage them take up more than an hour of your day, or cause you significant distress even outside of the moments when they're happening?

Gosh, an hour... you know, I’ve never actually sat down with a stopwatch or looked at the clock specifically to track it, so I really couldn't give you a definite yes or no on the exact amount of time. I mean, if I try to add it up right now... in the mornings, like I was saying, I'm trying to get out the door by 7:15, and I probably spend, what, maybe ten or fifteen extra minutes doing my rounds with the hair straightener and the coffee maker and the front door locks. And then at the end of the school day, around 3:45, I'm in my classroom checking the supply bins and the scissors and my desk. Which, by the way, I also always have to make sure the kids put the caps back on the glue sticks properly, because last year we had a whole batch dry out and it was just an absolute nightmare trying to get the front office to approve a purchase order for more mid-semester, they are so strict about the budget... anyway, that afternoon check is probably another ten minutes? Or maybe fifteen if I get stuck re-checking the confidential student notes? 

And then at my aunt's house in the evening with her daily pill organizer and making sure the stove dials are pointing straight up... that might be another ten or twelve minutes. So, I don't know, is that forty minutes total? Maybe forty-five? But then there's the time in the car when I'm silently replaying the images in my head, like picturing my hand turning the stove knob or closing the drawer. I don't even know how to count that time because I'm driving while I'm doing it, so I'm doing two things at once. Does that count towards the hour? I'm really not sure. I just haven't noticed if it crosses that one-hour mark exactly, because it's broken up into all these little chunks throughout my day. 

And as for causing me significant distress outside of those moments... I'm not entirely sure what you mean by "significant." Like, I'm not breaking down crying or having panic attacks or anything drastic when I'm just sitting at home or running errands. I'm still functioning fine. It's really just that lingering frustration I mentioned earlier. Like when I'm trying to use my colored pens and do my evening journaling, and I just can't get into the flow of it because my brain is still stuck on the image of my classroom or my aunt's kitchen. It's definitely a drag, and it makes me feel tired, but I don't know if I would use the word "distress" for it. It's more just this heavy, exhausting annoyance that buzzes in the background. So, yeah, I couldn't say for sure about it being a full hour or being actual distress.
Do you experience thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want or that upset you, even if you try not to have them?

Yeah, actually, that is exactly it. That’s really the whole reason I finally decided to make an appointment and come in to talk to someone. I just... I keep getting these incredibly nagging thoughts that I’ve forgotten something really, really important, and they just force their way into my head no matter what I'm doing. 

Like, with my aunt, I’ll be driving home from her house, or I'll be in the middle of making my own dinner, and suddenly this thought just slams into my brain that maybe I left her medicine out wrong. I'll start thinking, what if I left the blood pressure pills on the counter instead of putting them back in the cabinet, or what if I accidentally put the evening pills in the morning slot of her organizer? And I mean, I’ve been helping her with her medications for a long time now, so it’s a total routine for me, and logically I *know* I probably handled it perfectly fine. But the doubt just keeps popping back into my head, over and over, and I can't just brush it off. 

And it’s the exact same thing with my job. I’ll be sitting at home, trying to watch a show or do my journaling like I mentioned, and I’ll get this sudden, awful thought that I didn't set up my classroom materials safely before I left for the day. My brain will just start whispering, you know, what if you left the sharp adult scissors on the reading table instead of locking them in the top drawer of your desk? Or what if you left the paper cutter blade up? And even if I try to push the thought away, or I try to tell myself, 'No, you always put the scissors away, you know you do,' it just won't leave me alone. I try so hard not to have these thoughts, I really do try to just focus on my evening, but they just intrude anyway and make me second-guess every single move I made that day. It's just this constant loop of 'what if' that I can't seem to turn off.
Can you describe any specific actions or mental rituals you feel you must perform in response to these unwanted thoughts, even if they seem excessive or unrelated to the actual problem?

Well, yeah... I guess I do have a routine, if you want to call it that. It’s just that before I leave the house in the mornings, or before I leave my classroom at the end of the day, I really can't just grab my bag and walk out the door like a normal person. I end up having to go back over the exact same things a few times. 

Like, I know I already brought up the scissors and the straightener, but it really applies to a lot of things. In my classroom, I’ll pack up my bag, but then I have to go back and check my lesson plans. I have this big binder, right? And I have to flip through it and make sure everything is perfectly set for the next morning, and I’ll check it, close it, and then feel like I have to open it and check it again. And at my aunt's house, it's the same story. I don't just look at her pill organizer once. I have to physically go back and check that the little plastic lids are snapped shut tight, and I’ll check the stove knobs, just staring at them or touching them, over and over, maybe three or four times before I can even walk toward the front door. 

And then, if I’ve already left and I can't physically go back—like if I'm already driving down the road—I have to silently replay what I did in my head. I’ll just sit there at a red light and force myself to remember the exact feeling of closing the drawer or turning the stove dial, and I'll replay that little movie in my mind again and again. 

I just... I have to keep doing it, whether it's the physical checking or the mental replaying, until I finally feel this sort of shift in my brain. I have to do it until I feel calm enough to actually move on with my day. If I don't get that calm feeling, I just stay stuck in the loop, even though I know it makes me run late sometimes. Like I said before about practically sprinting down the hallway at school, or showing up late to meet a friend for coffee—it's because I was stuck at home going over the same things until my brain finally gave me permission to leave. It's incredibly frustrating, but I just can't seem to stop until I get that relief.

Do you feel that these thoughts or the things you do to manage them cause you significant stress, even if it's not extreme, or take up so much time that it feels like they're getting in the way of your regular routine?

I mean, like I was saying earlier about the distress part, I’m still getting through everything I need to do. I haven't missed a day of work, I'm still showing up every evening to help my aunt with her pills, and I'm keeping up with all my family commitments. I'm not falling apart. But... gosh, it really does put a lot of friction into my day. 

My mornings, especially, just take so much longer than they used to, or than they really should. I’ll have my alarm set, I’ll have my clothes laid out the night before to save time, but because I get caught up in doing all those little checks with the straightener and the locks and the coffee maker, I just watch the clock tick away. And then I'm practically flying out the door. By the time I actually pull into the school parking lot, grab my bags, and walk into my classroom, I just feel incredibly rushed. It’s like I’m already behind before the first bell even rings, before the kids even start piling in and asking me a million questions. It's just a really frantic, breathless way to start the day, and it takes me a while to shake that off.

And then it just sort of bleeds into everything else, you know? Like my lesson prep. I used to actually really enjoy sitting down and mapping out the week's activities, organizing the reading groups, getting all the materials ready. It used to be a smooth process, but now it just feels disjointed because I'm constantly distracted by those nagging thoughts. 

And my evening journaling... I know I brought that up a few minutes ago, but it really is a good example. I have these really nice colored pens and this beautiful journal, and sitting down with it is supposed to be my dedicated "me time." It's supposed to be how I unwind and clear my head after dealing with students all day. But lately, it just doesn't feel restorative at all. I sit there trying to write, and I just can't get into that peaceful headspace because I'm so mentally tired from managing all the checking and the mental replaying all day long. So, I guess, yes, it is getting in the way of my routine. I'm still checking all the boxes of what I need to get done, but the actual experience of doing those things just doesn't feel as smooth or as enjoyable as it used to.
Do you feel anxious or upset if you're unable to complete your checking routines or if you try to stop thinking about these worries?

I... gosh, I'm not really sure how to answer that, honestly. Because I don't think I've ever actually been in a situation where I couldn't finish my routine. I mean, I always find a way to get it done, even if it means I'm rushing later or making myself late. 

Like, I remember one time, maybe a couple of weeks ago, the school custodian, Mr. Henderson, came into my room to empty the trash right when I was doing my final walk-through before heading home. He’s super chatty, always wants to talk about his grandkids, which is really sweet—he has a grandson who just started playing T-ball, and he's so proud of him, he always has pictures on his phone to show me—but I was right in the middle of checking the scissors drawer. And instead of just grabbing my bag and leaving like a normal person, or just stopping my checks, I just stood there by the desk and nodded along with his whole story about the game until he finally tied up the trash bag and left. I just waited him out so I could finish checking the drawer and the cabinet. 

So I wasn't really prevented from doing it, you know? I just delayed it. I honestly don't know what would happen or how I'd feel if a fire alarm went off or if someone literally dragged me away before I was done, because that just hasn't happened. I just always make sure I finish. 

And as for trying to stop thinking about the worries... I haven't really noticed getting anxious or upset specifically because I'm *trying* to stop. It's more just that the thoughts are already there, and I don't know if pushing them away makes me feel anything extra. I've never really paid attention to that part of it, to be honest. I just know they keep popping up regardless of what I do. So, yeah, I guess I'm just not sure about that, because I always end up finishing what my brain wants me to do anyway.

Like, I'm not breaking down crying or having panic attacks or anything drastic when I'm just sitting at home or running errands. I'm still functioning fine. It's really just that lingering frustration I mentioned earlier. Like when I'm trying to use my colored pens and do my evening journaling, and I just can't get into the flow of it because my brain is still stuck on the image of my classroom or my aunt's kitchen. It's definitely a drag, and it makes me feel tired, but I don't know if I would use the word "distress" for it. It's more just this heavy, exhausting annoyance that buzzes in the background. So, yeah, I couldn't say for sure about it being a full hour or being actual distress.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences intrusive, unwanted thoughts that cause anxiety or distress, a key feature of obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.2).
doctor.question: Do you experience thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want or that upset you, even if you try not to have them?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep getting these nagging thoughts that I forgot something important, like leaving my aunt’s medicine out wrong or not setting up my classroom materials safely, and even when I know I probably handled it, the doubt keeps popping back into my head.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unwanted, upsetting thoughts that intrude into the mind despite attempts not to have them, which directly corresponds to the definition of Obsessions.

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually, that is exactly it. That’s really the whole reason I finally decided to make an appointment and come in to talk to someone. I just... I keep getting these incredibly nagging thoughts that I’ve forgotten something really, really important, and they just force their way into my head no matter what I'm doing. 

Like, with my aunt, I’ll be driving home from her house, or I'll be in the middle of making my own dinner, and suddenly this thought just slams into my brain that maybe I left her medicine out wrong. I'll start thinking, what if I left the blood pressure pills on the counter instead of putting them back in the cabinet, or what if I accidentally put the evening pills in the morning slot of her organizer? And I mean, I’ve been helping her with her medications for a long time now, so it’s a total routine for me, and logically I *know* I probably handled it perfectly fine. But the doubt just keeps popping back into my head, over and over, and I can't just brush it off. 

And it’s the exact same thing with my job. I’ll be sitting at home, trying to watch a show or do my journaling like I mentioned, and I’ll get this sudden, awful thought that I didn't set up my classroom materials safely before I left for the day. My brain will just start whispering, you know, what if you left the sharp adult scissors on the reading table instead of locking them in the top drawer of your desk? Or what if you left the paper cutter blade up? And even if I try to push the thought away, or I try to tell myself, 'No, you always put the scissors away, you know you do,' it just won't leave me alone. I try so hard not to have these thoughts, I really do try to just focus on my evening, but they just intrude anyway and make me second-guess every single move I made that day. It's just this constant loop of 'what if' that I can't seem to turn off.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences compulsive behaviors or mental acts in response to obsessive thoughts that are not logically connected or are clearly excessive.
doctor.question: Can you describe any specific actions or mental rituals you feel you must perform in response to these unwanted thoughts, even if they seem excessive or unrelated to the actual problem?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: Before I leave the house or my classroom, I’ll go back over the same things a few times—checking the pill organizer, the stove, my lesson plans, or silently replaying what I did—until I feel calm enough to move on, even though it makes me run late sometimes.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about specific actions or mental rituals performed in response to unwanted thoughts, which directly maps to the 'Compulsions' symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah... I guess I do have a routine, if you want to call it that. It’s just that before I leave the house in the mornings, or before I leave my classroom at the end of the day, I really can't just grab my bag and walk out the door like a normal person. I end up having to go back over the exact same things a few times. 

Like, I know I already brought up the scissors and the straightener, but it really applies to a lot of things. In my classroom, I’ll pack up my bag, but then I have to go back and check my lesson plans. I have this big binder, right? And I have to flip through it and make sure everything is perfectly set for the next morning, and I’ll check it, close it, and then feel like I have to open it and check it again. And at my aunt's house, it's the same story. I don't just look at her pill organizer once. I have to physically go back and check that the little plastic lids are snapped shut tight, and I’ll check the stove knobs, just staring at them or touching them, over and over, maybe three or four times before I can even walk toward the front door. 

And then, if I’ve already left and I can't physically go back—like if I'm already driving down the road—I have to silently replay what I did in my head. I’ll just sit there at a red light and force myself to remember the exact feeling of closing the drawer or turning the stove dial, and I'll replay that little movie in my mind again and again. 

I just... I have to keep doing it, whether it's the physical checking or the mental replaying, until I finally feel this sort of shift in my brain. I have to do it until I feel calm enough to actually move on with my day. If I don't get that calm feeling, I just stay stuck in the loop, even though I know it makes me run late sometimes. Like I said before about practically sprinting down the hallway at school, or showing up late to meet a friend for coffee—it's because I was stuck at home going over the same things until my brain finally gave me permission to leave. It's incredibly frustrating, but I just can't seem to stop until I get that relief.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences compulsions that are time-consuming or cause clinically significant distress or impairment.
doctor.question: Do you feel that these thoughts or the things you do to manage them cause you significant stress, even if it's not extreme, or take up so much time that it feels like they're getting in the way of your regular routine?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting through work and family commitments, but my mornings take longer and I sometimes arrive at school feeling rushed or behind before the day even starts. Lesson prep and my evening journaling don’t feel as smooth or restorative as they used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the level of stress or interference with my regular routine caused by the thoughts and behaviors, which directly addresses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I mean, like I was saying earlier about the distress part, I’m still getting through everything I need to do. I haven't missed a day of work, I'm still showing up every evening to help my aunt with her pills, and I'm keeping up with all my family commitments. I'm not falling apart. But... gosh, it really does put a lot of friction into my day. 

My mornings, especially, just take so much longer than they used to, or than they really should. I’ll have my alarm set, I’ll have my clothes laid out the night before to save time, but because I get caught up in doing all those little checks with the straightener and the locks and the coffee maker, I just watch the clock tick away. And then I'm practically flying out the door. By the time I actually pull into the school parking lot, grab my bags, and walk into my classroom, I just feel incredibly rushed. It’s like I’m already behind before the first bell even rings, before the kids even start piling in and asking me a million questions. It's just a really frantic, breathless way to start the day, and it takes me a while to shake that off.

And then it just sort of bleeds into everything else, you know? Like my lesson prep. I used to actually really enjoy sitting down and mapping out the week's activities, organizing the reading groups, getting all the materials ready. It used to be a smooth process, but now it just feels disjointed because I'm constantly distracted by those nagging thoughts. 

And my evening journaling... I know I brought that up a few minutes ago, but it really is a good example. I have these really nice colored pens and this beautiful journal, and sitting down with it is supposed to be my dedicated "me time." It's supposed to be how I unwind and clear my head after dealing with students all day. But lately, it just doesn't feel restorative at all. I sit there trying to write, and I just can't get into that peaceful headspace because I'm so mentally tired from managing all the checking and the mental replaying all day long. So, I guess, yes, it is getting in the way of my routine. I'm still checking all the boxes of what I need to get done, but the actual experience of doing those things just doesn't feel as smooth or as enjoyable as it used to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences anxiety or distress specifically related to not performing the rituals or suppressing the obsessive thoughts, which would support a diagnosis of OCD (F42.2) over GAD (F43.22).
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or upset if you're unable to complete your checking routines or if you try to stop thinking about these worries?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the anxiety or distress experienced when compulsions are resisted or obsessions are suppressed. While this relates to the mechanism of compulsions (preventing anxiety), it does not match a new, unaddressed symptom in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
I... gosh, I'm not really sure how to answer that, honestly. Because I don't think I've ever actually been in a situation where I couldn't finish my routine. I mean, I always find a way to get it done, even if it means I'm rushing later or making myself late. 

Like, I remember one time, maybe a couple of weeks ago, the school custodian, Mr. Henderson, came into my room to empty the trash right when I was doing my final walk-through before heading home. He’s super chatty, always wants to talk about his grandkids, which is really sweet—he has a grandson who just started playing T-ball, and he's so proud of him, he always has pictures on his phone to show me—but I was right in the middle of checking the scissors drawer. And instead of just grabbing my bag and leaving like a normal person, or just stopping my checks, I just stood there by the desk and nodded along with his whole story about the game until he finally tied up the trash bag and left. I just waited him out so I could finish checking the drawer and the cabinet. 

So I wasn't really prevented from doing it, you know? I just delayed it. I honestly don't know what would happen or how I'd feel if a fire alarm went off or if someone literally dragged me away before I was done, because that just hasn't happened. I just always make sure I finish. 

And as for trying to stop thinking about the worries... I haven't really noticed getting anxious or upset specifically because I'm *trying* to stop. It's more just that the thoughts are already there, and I don't know if pushing them away makes me feel anything extra. I've never really paid attention to that part of it, to be honest. I just know they keep popping up regardless of what I do. So, yeah, I guess I'm just not sure about that, because I always end up finishing what my brain wants me to do anyway.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms align more closely with OCD, specifically with checking compulsions and intrusive thoughts causing significant functional impairment. No other disorders fit the clinical picture as well.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent, intrusive, and distressing thoughts related to potential harm to others (students, aunt) due to perceived lapses in responsibility, accompanied by repetitive behaviors (checking, mental replay) aimed at reducing distress or preventing a feared event. These symptoms cause clinically significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning, despite preserved overall functioning. The content and structure of the symptoms align with obsessive-compulsive disorder, predominantly obsessive type.
